narrative_purpose: Make the chapter's counterintuitive soil-carbon claim visible: microbial remains can persist longer than the leaf material they consumed because access, aggregation and mineral binding protect them.
subject: A single magnified Pandoran soil aggregate shown in cutaway around the softened edge of a fallen leaf. At upper left, fragments of blue-green leaf tissue are being taken into small rod-shaped and spherical microbial cells along a thin water film. Deeper inside the aggregate, broken cell walls and translucent microbial residues lie pressed tightly against broad clay plates and rusty metal-oxide grains, while another residue pocket is sealed behind interlocked mineral grains. Fresh leaf fragments remain exposed near the surface; the protected microbial remnants occupy the quiet mineral interior.
scene: The microscopic interior of damp forest soil beneath the chapter's recurring fallen leaf, isolated against a deep indigo specimen field.
camera: Straight-on macro cutaway, with active decomposition in the upper-left third and three clearly readable protected residue sites across the lower and right interior.
light: Faint cyan on fresh leaf fragments and water films, living teal on active cells, muted amber on microbial residues, and soft mineral-grey highlights on clay and oxide surfaces; the sealed pore remains darker.
palette: Void indigo background, charcoal and mineral grey soil, cyan water and leaf veins, living teal cells, restrained amber residue and iron-oxide accents.
style: Painterly soil-biogeochemistry naturalist plate with tactile mineral and membrane textures, scientifically observed rather than infographic-clean.
detail_level: Crisp microbial cells, torn cell-wall residues, clay plates, oxide grains, water films and the sealed aggregate pocket; surrounding soil fades into uncluttered darkness.
composition: A continuous diagonal transition from recognizable leaf tissue to living microbes to mineral-bound and physically enclosed microbial remains, with clear open margins for later interface annotation.
consistency_notes: Continue the fallen-leaf and soil-pore material language from figures 01 and 02. The long-lived material must read as fragmented microbial residue physically protected by minerals, not as intact immortal organisms or magical amber fossils.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no arrows, no molecular formulae, no recycling icon, no anthropomorphic microbes, no vector infographic, no photographic or glossy 3D-render look, no cartoon style
